Replay

Negotiated snapshot parts

7 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Negotiated LZ4 deltasNegotiated two-erasure paritySchema-derived array shuffle

Use negotiated snapshot parts to send large snapshots as bounded unreliable datagrams after bootstrap. The initial snapshot still establishes a reliable baseline. After that, a capable recipient can receive full or delta snapshots in pieces without waiting for the previous large snapshot's acknowledgment. Reliable facts remain the confirmation gate.

The protocol-7 base contract, existing packet schemas, canonical state bytes and checkpoint format are unchanged. The optional Features packet (kind 16) carries generation, Welcome serial, feature bits and maximum part size. Bit 0 offers snapshot parts. The sender chooses the smaller advertised/configured limit, between 512 and 1,024 bytes, including the envelope. Capability and transfer state are discarded on the next Welcome/recovery scope. Before its first pump a client may set snapshot_parts_enabled = false to use the fallback path.

A server sends Snapshot_Part (kind 17) only after a valid capability message from that exact admitted connection, generation and serial. A frozen pre-extension Replay runner interoperates in both directions: the older server ignores the unknown optional advertisement; the newer server keeps the existing snapshot path for an older client. The compatibility corpus verifies identical base contract hashes and advancing worlds. This does not change interoperability with Kit or older Replay protocol versions.

Each part has the ordinary schema envelope plus generation, serial, snapshot ID, whole-message digest, total byte count, part index and chosen part size. The inner message is the exact existing full/delta snapshot envelope. A receiver validates scope, size, offsets and duplicate consistency before copying. Complete reassembly must match the digest, inner kind/scope/tick/ID, then pass the existing canonical snapshot/delta decoder, state validation and baseline checks. Partial or corrupt messages never publish a world or authorize a new baseline.

The sender retains at most one encoded message per recipient. Backpressure resumes its remaining parts before encoding another world. Reserved IDs are never reused when a checkpoint or lost baseline abandons a partial send. Cache/acknowledgment eligibility begins after all data parts have been accepted by the transport, before final parity parts if those are still clearing backpressure. Facts are sent first, and existing byte/rate budgets apply to every part and its overhead.

A client retains at most four incomplete assemblies, each bounded by its actual snapshot wire size and the 64-KiB transport limit. Newer IDs can evict older partial assemblies; completed/stale assemblies are discarded, and incomplete ones expire after two seconds. Reordering and identical duplicate parts are allowed. Assembly metadata supports up to 256 parts, including the smallest negotiated datagrams. Reset/destroy frees assembly memory. A sender's reusable wire buffer may retain its peak capacity until server destruction; it holds at most one snapshot per peer.

This improves delivery opportunity, not bandwidth efficiency. At an unchanged snapshot cadence, more complete worlds can arrive and more correction work can run. Packet overhead and loss probability also increase with fragmentation. Use the existing snapshot cadence, egress budgets and recipient projection controls; measure the actual game. Delivery still depends on transport queues, peer credit, loss, CPU and available bandwidth. Bootstrap/facts are reliable, and losing a needed delta baseline still requests the existing full-snapshot recovery path.

Stats.fragmented_snapshots, snapshot_parts_sent, snapshot_parts_received and snapshot_parts_expired expose activity. Application byte counters include part envelopes; transport framing/retransmission remains outside them. These counters and capability/assembly buffers are local runtime state, not checkpoint state.

Tests cover advancing dense worlds versus fallback, loss/jitter/duplication, backpressure, complete-only publication, scope/digest/ID corruption, bounded assembly eviction/expiry, smaller negotiated packet limits and reconnects. The frozen-runner corpus checks the protocol-7 interoperability claim. Real swarm, browser/RTC and migration results are recorded separately in the roadmap evidence.

Negotiated LZ4 deltas#

Feature bit 1 adds Snapshot_Delta_Lz4 (kind 18), using the existing 48-byte delta prefix followed by an independent LZ4 block of canonical XOR bytes. The acknowledged base ID/hash and target hash remain mandatory. The block has an exact decoded size from the snapshot schema, with complete validation before output. Full and sparse-delta encodings remain available. The sender chooses LZ4 only when it is strictly smaller than both, and skips attempts that cannot meet a conservative format-size lower bound. The same message may use ordinary unreliable delivery or snapshot parts, according to size and negotiated support.

Client.lz4_snapshots_enabled = false before first pump advertises parts without LZ4. snapshot_parts_enabled = false retains the base-protocol fallback. A client refuses an LZ4 message when support was not advertised. Capabilities reset with the Welcome scope and are absent from checkpoints. Stats.lz4_snapshots counts successful messages. The sender reuses bounded scratch: a 16-KiB match table and a 65,808-byte output stage, with no retained dictionary. There is no foreign compression library in the runtime.

The codec contract and reference corpus cover the format and error behavior. Frozen pre-extension and parts-only runners are both exercised by the compatibility gate. Canonical state and base contract hashes are unchanged; this extension reduces encoded payload, not game state or the history needed to reproduce simulation and historical queries.

Godot sessions expose the local Session_Options.disable_lz4 preference, copied through Room reconnect/migration setup. It does not change game state or the checkpoint contract. Scrapyard's RSY_LZ4=0 development setting uses that option; the browser acceptance party keeps one parts-only peer to test both encodings.

Negotiated two-erasure parity#

Feature bit 4 (value 16) enables Snapshot_Parity (kind 23). For every group of up to eight data parts, the sender emits two parity parts, interleaved after that group's data. They protect the exact existing inner snapshot bytes. Each parity packet uses the existing part header; its index is group * 2 + row, where row 0 is P and row 1 is Q from the erasure codec. Short data parts are virtually zero-padded to the longest part in their group.

The receiver can reconstruct any two missing shards among that group's data and parity. It then performs the same whole-message digest, canonical decoder, baseline and state checks as ordinary reassembly. Parity carries no authority to publish incomplete or unvalidated state. Duplicate consistency, generation, Welcome serial, epoch/content, ID and size checks apply before reconstruction. An older peer never receives parity unless it offered the feature.

Every parity packet consumes existing sender byte/rate credit and uses the negotiated packet size. Full eight-part groups add 25% shard overhead; shorter final groups have a higher proportional cost. This can reduce snapshot cadence under the same budget, even as it improves completion under loss. More than two erasures within one group may still prevent recovery; later snapshots and resync remain available. This is not a guarantee against arbitrary loss or queue overload.

Each of the four client assemblies lazily owns parity storage bounded by 2 * ceil(data_parts / 8) * payload_bytes, in addition to its existing data. The existing wire-size, assembly-count and expiry limits remain. Reset, expiry, eviction and destruction free parity together with data. The sender needs only 2 KiB of stack scratch per flush and retains no extra snapshot history.

Parity is enabled by default for capable peers. Set Client.snapshot_erasure_enabled = false before its first pump, or Session_Options.disable_snapshot_erasure = true, to opt out. Scrapyard exposes RSY_FEC=0 (browser query fec=0) for comparison. These are local transport preferences, not durable gameplay data or changes to the base protocol contract.

Stats.snapshot_parity_sent, snapshot_parity_received, snapshot_parity_bytes and snapshot_shards_recovered report the extra activity. Recovered shards can include reordered data, so the recovery count is not a direct packet-loss count.

Schema-derived array shuffle#

Feature bit 5 (value 32) offers Snapshot_Delta_Shuffled (kind 24), alongside parts and ordinary LZ4 support. Its existing 48-byte delta prefix is followed by an eight-byte little-endian Schema.shuffle_fingerprint and an LZ4 block of the shuffled canonical XOR. The receiver requires that signature to match its compiled transform, then reconstructs canonical bytes and checks the usual base/target hashes, scope, snapshot ID and state. Fragmentation and parity protect the encoded message unchanged.

The schema transform groups equal byte positions from fixed-array records. It changes no gameplay values, query history, canonical fingerprints or checkpoint bytes. The sender retains the old full/sparse/LZ4 choices and uses this candidate only when it saves bytes after its extra signature. A size heuristic skips already compact candidates; see the codec and scratch contract.

Scratch is lazy and reused: twice the canonical snapshot size per server and per receiving client, freed at destruction. Stats.shuffled_snapshots counts accepted messages, shuffle_attempts counts candidate encodes, and shuffle_bytes_saved counts logical payload savings relative to the prior candidate for accepted messages. These savings exclude changes in part/parity/framing overhead and are not a measured reduction in total network traffic. lz4_snapshots includes both ordinary and shuffled LZ4 messages.

Set Client.snapshot_shuffle_enabled = false before first pump, or Session_Options.disable_snapshot_shuffle = true, to opt out. Scrapyard exposes RSY_SHUFFLE=0 (browser query shuffle=0) for measurement. A peer that does not advertise the capability receives its existing formats. The base protocol contract and content semantics remain unchanged; the transform has a separate versioned signature so an ordinary schema match cannot authorize a different permutation.
